item.title: Dynamical-Model-Informed Stochastic Flow Matching for Global Probabilistic Subseasonal Forecasting of Means and Extremes
item.description: arXiv:2610.30159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-based models provide skillful subseasonal forecasts but suffer from systematic biases, weakened teleconnections, and parameterized physics, while very large ensembles remain computationally expensive. Purely data-driven models also see too few realizations of the low-frequency modes that provide subseasonal predictability. We introduce methodname, a hybrid framework that converts modelshort subseasonal ensemble guidance into 90-member stochastic forecasts of weekly precipitation and 2 m temperature on a global 1-degree grid using a lead-aware flow-matching U-Net. Its stochastic prior initializes members with EOF perturbations conditioned on the Madden-Julian Oscillation, North Atlantic Oscillation, El Nino-Southern Oscillation, and lead week, allowing the learned flow to refine large-scale covariance rather than create it from white noise. On held-out 2021-2025 forecasts, empirical CRPS improves by 22.0% for precipitation and 25.6% for temperature in a same-initialization four-versus-four comparison, and by 32.2% and 34.0% in the 90-versus-four production comparison. Ablations across five training seeds show distinct gains from the structured prior and a learned error-variance pathway, with the prior contributing more. Verification over 120 observed-extreme cases shows positive CRPS skill, but the ensemble remains underdispersive, four-member upper quantiles are poorly resolved, and precipitation exceedance BSS is near neutral after week 1. Results support improved probabilistic skill and tail representation, but not calibrated operational rare-event probabilities. Case studies of the 2022 UK heatwave, 2023 California atmospheric rivers, and 2022 Pakistan floods illustrate the reach and limits of dynamically informed refinement.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah A. Fahad, Manmeet Singh

item.title: Cleaner air strengthens the Pacific trade winds without a detectable change in El Nino
item.description: arXiv:2610.31236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Air quality policy will cut aerosol and ozone precursor emissions, and studies disagree on how the tropical Pacific circulation and the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) will respond. Here we show, in 12 Earth system models with and without air quality controls, that the cuts strengthen the Pacific trade winds and offset half to two thirds of the weakening projected without them. The response is absent with prescribed sea surface temperatures and detectable only after 2040. It is consistent with the Indian Ocean warming relative to the Pacific, which also ranks the responses to cuts made region by region. ENSO amplitude changes by less than a tenth of its value, the smallest change this ensemble could detect. The change implied by the mean state shift is a sixth of that, and an ENSO model trained without the reduced emission runs predicts none. El Nino's regional impacts still change, because the background climate does.
item.dc:creator: Ioana Colfescu, Alice Pigelet, Chen Lu, Massimo A. Bollasina, Silvio Gualdi

item.title: Can We Trust Evaluations of AI Weather Forecasts for Extremes? How Evaluation Protocols Shape Model Rankings
item.description: arXiv:2610.31237v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI weather models perform competitively with traditional physics-based models at a fraction of the computational cost, and they are thus already used operationally. However, studies reach conflicting conclusions about their ability to forecast extreme weather events, and comparisons across studies are complicated by differing evaluation protocols. We discuss the challenges that arise when comparing AI and physics-based weather forecasts for extreme events. Within a common experimental design, we find that model rankings are highly sensitive to the choice of evaluation metrics: the considered physics-based model tends to perform best when evaluation is restricted to observed extreme events, whereas AI models generally perform better when evaluated using weighted scoring functions. A contingency table analysis shows that AI models underpredict the frequency of extremes, so that their scores are generally dominated by misses, while the physics-based model forecasts extremes more frequently and its scores are dominated by false alarms. Different evaluation metrics penalise these errors differently. Further score decompositions confirm that the score differences arise primarily from miscalibration rather than discrimination ability. This sheds light on the contrasting results in the literature, and highlights the importance of the evaluation metrics used to evaluate AI models.
item.dc:creator: Tobias Biegert, Sam Allen, Zhongwei Zhang, Sebastian Lerch

item.title: OTProf: estimating high-resolution profiles of optical turbulence ($C_n^2$) from reanalysis using deep learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.09346v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate, high-resolution vertical profiles of optical turbulence ($C_n^2$), which reflect local meteorology and topography, are crucial for ground-based optical astronomy and free-space optical communication. However, measuring these profiles or generating them with numerical weather models requires substantial operational or computational effort. In this work, we present OTProf, a deep-learning method that estimates high-resolution $C_n^2$ profiles from widely available coarse-resolution ERA5 reanalysis data. OTProf is based on the Squeezeformer architecture, modified for super-resolution by introducing grid-agnostic interpolation in the latent space. We train and evaluate OTProf in the Netherlands using high-resolution $C_n^2$ data obtained from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. The commonly used Hufnagel-Valley model serves as the baseline. Overall, OTProf reproduces the vertical structure of WRF-based $C_n^2$ more accurately than Hufnagel-Valley and yields more accurate estimates of the Fried parameter $r_0$ and the scintillation index $\sigma_I^2$. Out-of-domain performance is assessed using a smaller WRF-based $C_n^2$ dataset covering the Canary Islands. Initial results indicate a performance drop because the orography differs markedly from the training domain. We show that output bias correction based on a few local simulations can help OTProf to adapt, but more work for domain adaptation is needed. OTProf is therefore primarily recommended for in-domain applications, e.g., generating $C_n^2$ climatologies from long ERA5 records.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Pierzyna, Sukanta Basu, Rudolf Saathof

item.title: State-resolved multimodal contributions to stratospheric polar vortex predictability
item.description: arXiv:2605.13417v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The dynamical basis of stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) predictability remains unclear, particularly the relative roles of persistence, structural variability, and cross-level coupling. Here we combine eigen microstate theory with mesoscopic Granger-causality analysis of ERA5 geopotential height fields to quantify the predictive contributions of eigen microstates. We show that short-term predictability is dominated by the persistence of the leading stratospheric state, whereas higher-order stratospheric structures and tropospheric variability provide additional predictive information at subseasonal leads. Including these additional states increases the all-winter 30-day prediction correlation from 0.24 to 0.33 and reduces forecast error. These contributions exhibit strong lead-time dependence and vary between winters with and without sudden stratospheric warmings. Part of this predictive information overlaps with that contained in preceding 100 hPa eddy heat flux, linking state-resolved predictability to wave-related circulation variability. Our results unify SPV predictability within a multimodal, state-resolved framework and provide a physically interpretable pathway.
item.dc:creator: Shuo Yang, Dan Zhao, Tingting Xue, Chunhua Zeng, Yongwen Zhang, Xiaosong Chen
